newsitem.title: GERMANY: CompuServe just first case in German cyber-crusade.
newsitem.headline: CompuServe just first case in German cyber-crusade.

text.p: Germany's Internet industry expects more indictments to follow after Bavarian authorities filed charges against online service CompuServe Inc, marking a decisive turning point in the debate over Internet regulation.

Just as the German parliament is set to begin debating legislation that takes a liberal view of policing cyberspace, prosecutors appear to be using CompuServe to set an example meant to urge lawmakers to take a harder line.

"There is hardly an online service or internet service provider in Germany today that has not been the subject of an criminal investigation," said Michael Schneider, an attorney who specialises in computer law.
"Now that these charges have been raised I presume others will follow. CompuServe will not be the last case," he added.

While censorship of Internet providers is commonplace in countries such as China and Singapore, Germany appears to be the first Western democracy to serve an indictment against an online service for Internet content considered illegal.

In the case of CompuServe, prosecutors indicted Felix Somm, head of its Central European operations, for aiding in the trafficking of child pornography, dissemination of Nazi symbols and violent computer games that are illegal in Germany.
"CompuServe Inc considers the charges against Herr Somm to be baseless and expects that in the end there will be no conviction," the company said in a statement.

This case marks the culmination of police activities over the past year which have included raids on the offices of online services as investigators seek to determine who should be held responsible for crimes committed online.
Investigations against CompuServe began in 1995 and the company then took the unprecedented step of banning access to millions of its members worldwide to over 200 newsgroups.

The move caused an outcry among CompuServe users and cyber-rights groups in the United States, who were outraged that German authorities could exercise such influence over what Americans were able to read and view online.

German police have teams of cybersleuths looking for evidence of Internet crime, especially child sex rings or extremist literature such as neo-Nazi writings or the recent banning of left-wing magazine Radikal.
The online industry argues that providers should be viewed as telecommunications carriers rather than publishers who are held liable for what is printed in their publications.

"No one would ever bring charges against (phone company) Deutsche Telekom for crimes committed over the telephone," said Schneider. "The problem is that it is not clearly defined how far the responsibility of service providers goes."

America Online's German subsidiary, AOL Deutschland, was investigated by Hamburg authorities last year, but no charges were filed. The Deutsche Forschungsnetz (DFN), a scientific research network that offers public Internet access, has been forced to block access to a Dutch site on the World Wide Web which hosted the banned magazine Radikal.

While German online services and internet access providers are making an effort to cooperate with authorities, they remain convinced that they cannot control the wilds of cyberspace and should not be held responsible for illicit Web sites.
"We can take responsibility for the content that we produce ourselves but not for that which can be found on the World Wide Web or in newsgroups," said Ingo Reese, AOL spokesman.

EUnet Deutschland GmbH, Germany's largest Internet service provider, said German authorities were clearly stepping up Internet investigations. EUnet plans to block minors using its service from accessing certain newsgroups.

Germany's draft Information and Communications Services Bill, which comes up for debate in parliament on Friday, states that internet service providers should not be made generally responsible for content on the Internet.

It is one of the first efforts in Europe to define Internet regulation and events in Germany are being watched closely by the European Commission, which has yet to draft any European directive on the issue of Internet regulation.
